newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Ministers grapple with Euro pact before EU summit.
newsitem.headline: Ministers grapple with Euro pact before EU summit.

text.p: European finance ministers struggled into the early hours on Friday to stop a row over a single currency from overshadowing a summit of EU leaders designed to map out the European Union of the 21st century.

In a last minute bid to clinch an agreement, the Irish hosts of an emergency meeting of Europe's top financial officials launched a new proposal aimed a bridging a yawning gap between Germany and its European parners over future budgetary rigour.
At issue is Germany's demand that countries inside a single currency system be subject to fines for running excessive government deficits.

Bonn wants water-tight language to force countries to be disciplined by a stability pact making sure they pursue tight fiscal policies once they have signed up to European economic and monetary union (EMU). Its partners are seeking some leeway.
The new proposal would meet German demands for a specific figure to define when an economic downswing could save countries with excessive deficits from facing EU fines.
But it would also leave the last word on whether fine was imposed to EU ministers.
It was not clear whether the ministers would seal an agreement before the EU summit or be forced to hand the problem over to EU leaders meeting on Friday.

The aim of the finance ministers' meeting had been to clear the decks for the EU leaders and allow them to concentrate on the business of discussing the shape of a Europe with at least 10 new members, mainly from the former Communist east.

Failure to clinch an accord over the next few days would also upset financial markets where there is concern that disagreement over the details of a single currency might throw the whole concept into doubt.
The stability pact is a key element of a report on EMU due to be studied by EU leaders at the summit proper.

Other aspects of the report have already been informally agreed. They include the legal basis for the euro and a new post-EMU exchange rate mechanism to keep EU currencies outside the euro bloc stable.
The EU leaders were also due to discuss at the summit the bloc's long-term future, in the shape of a draft EU treaty written by the Irish EU presidency.
"What we are aspiring towards is bringing Europe closer together. We want to see a closer union of the peoples of Europe," Irish Prime Minister and summit host John Bruton said.

The Irish draft treaty shows the majority of countries are heading towards closer cooperation in crime fighting, joint employment policies, stronger foreign policy links and a true border-free Europe with common asylum and immigration policies.
It also calls on the EU to create an area of freedom, security and justice ensuring the free movement of people.

Of all the leaders coming to Dublin, British Prime Minister John Major will be among the most watched. With his ruling Conservative party torn apart over Europe, Major will be under pressure not to appear too conciliatory to his EU colleagues.
Britain opposes most of the proposals under discussion for the draft treaty -- which is supposed to prepare the bloc for enlargement into central and eastern Europe.
London also has an opt-out on the single currency, making discussions on post-EMU life something of a political minefield for the embattled British leader.
